comment: The document makes consent the main way individuals control their health data (Section 2.3, p.34–35), lists a "health-sector consent service" in Table 2.2, and tells several components to "integrate with consent management services" (for example the Lifelong Health Record, req #14). But consent is the only one of these capabilities with no component write-up and no functional requirements. The twelve other components each get a full specification; the consent service they all rely on does not. Implementers are told to connect to something the guidance never defines, which risks consent being recorded but not consistently enforced.

public.text: The document makes consent the main way individuals control their health data (Section 2.3, p.34–35), lists a "health-sector consent service" in Table 2.2, and tells several components to "integrate with consent management services" (for example the Lifelong Health Record, req #14). But consent is the only one of these capabilities with no component write-up and no functional requirements. The twelve other components each get a full specification; the consent service they all rely on does not. Implementers are told to connect to something the guidance never defines, which risks consent being recorded but not consistently enforced.
public.suggestedRevision: Give the consent service its own component description with functional requirements, at the same level of detail as the other components: what a consent record contains, how consent is checked at the point of data exchange, how a withdrawal takes effect across systems, and how it works with a national cross-sector consent service where one exists.
